questions.question: Resolve the water-diamond paradox in your own words, using the concepts of value in use, value in exchange and scarcity.
questions.expected_answer: Water has enormous value in use — life depends on it — but tiny value in exchange, while diamonds have little value in use and enormous value in exchange. The paradox resolves because exchange value is governed by scarcity relative to wants and by the utility of the next unit, not by total usefulness. Water is abundant, so one more glass adds almost nothing for someone with plenty; diamonds are rare, so even one more is prized. Abundance makes things cheap and scarcity makes them dear, regardless of how essential the good is.

questions.question: List the conditions of a perfect market, and explain how the failure of these conditions produces the three imperfect market structures.
questions.expected_answer: A perfect market needs many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, perfect knowledge, and free entry and exit — making everyone a price taker. When the number of sellers collapses to one, a monopoly forms and the seller becomes a price maker. When only a few large sellers remain, watching each other, an oligopoly forms. When many sellers remain but the product is differentiated by brand, location or style, monopolistic competition forms, giving each seller a small slice of pricing power. The fewer the sellers and the higher the entry barriers, the further the price drifts from the perfect benchmark.

questions.question: Name the five functions of markets and illustrate each with an example from this lesson.
questions.expected_answer: Price formation: demand and supply meeting at the tomato market's one going rate. Allocation: a rising price drawing labour and capital toward a product society wants more of. Information: one price acting as a compressed message about scarcity that millions read at once, like world gold prices on a phone screen. Rationing: a scarce good going to those willing and able to pay, as with festival water. Linking buyers and sellers: strangers connected through chains of markets, like the wool farmer and the tailor. In one sentence: markets form prices, and prices then allocate, inform, ration and connect.
